questions.stem: Name the antigen produced by each of the three ABO alleles.
questions.modelAnswer: IA produces antigen A, IB produces antigen B, and IO produces no antigens.
Codominance describes a genotype whose two alleles each leave a visible mark on the organism's traits.

questions.stem: Explain why a child of group O can be born to a group A parent and a group B parent.
questions.modelAnswer: Each parent can carry the IO allele alongside their main allele, so the child can inherit IO from both and, with no antigen A or antigen B made, belongs to group O.

questions.stem: A blood-group A parent and a blood-group B parent have a group O child. What genotypes must the parents carry, and what chance does another child have of group O?
questions.modelAnswer: Each parent is heterozygous, carrying IO with their codominant partner allele, so each pregnancy has a one-in-four, or 25 percent, chance of a group O child.

questions.stem: List the four offspring genotypes shown by the IAIO by IBIO square.
questions.modelAnswer: The combinations are IAIB, IAIO, IBIO and IOIO, each occupying one cell of the diagram.

questions.modelAnswer: The chance is one cell out of four, so 25 percent.

questions.stem: Explain why knowing a child's blood group can reveal hidden parental genotypes.
questions.modelAnswer: A group O child must have received an IO allele from each parent, so each parent must carry IO even if their own phenotype is A or B.

questions.stem: Two parents, both IAIO, plan a family. Predict the possible offspring blood groups and the chance of group O.
questions.modelAnswer: The square gives IAIA, IAIO and IOIO outcomes, so children may be group A or group O, with a 25 percent chance for group O.
